messages.subject: [statnet_help] parallel update
messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet community,

I have a question about profiling parallel ergm code.  I fit dyadic dependent ERGM's in serial and parallel to networks of size 50, 500 and 5000; in each case, the mean degree was 15. The serial fit converged quickly, and for each network appeared to take far less time than the parallel (some details below).
Profiling ERGM fits for networks of size 5000, with mean degree = 15.

Serial fit
   user  system elapsed
174.584   0.132 174.790

Parallel fit (using 10 cpu's on multiple nodes)
      user  system elapsed
727.921   0.770 729.479

Parallel fit (using 16 cpu's on same node)
    user   system  elapsed
1236.118    1.310 1240.925

I find this result counterintuitive, because I expected the parallel fitting to take much less time. Can someone please help me figure out what might be wrong?

Thanks,
Aditya

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users

I would like to determine if there is a difference in
contributions/importance of different classes of nodes between three
directed advice networks.

Basically the data contain three separate networks for different types of
advice. The nodes differ with regards to one categorical attribute (five
distinct classes) and we assume that only nodes in one of these classes
would want to receive advice (let's call these"pupils", while all the
others are professionals of some kind). Pupils can receive advice from each
other, or from any of the other categories. There are 8 pupils and 20 other
nodes.

I'm thinking of modelling this as an ERGM, with a parameter for density and
a node attribute effect on indegree (links pointing where the advice came
from). "Forbidden" relations could be represented with structural zeros,
but my concern is that there are quite many of them. Would this
configuration violate any model assumptions? Or is there a different
approach that you would recommend?

Thanks in advance
Fabian

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fabian,

A TERGM (not STERGM) without any temporal dependencies can be applied to 
multiple separate groups. This essentially reduces to a pooled ERGM. 
Estimation is possible using the xergm package, which builds on many 
statnet functions. There are two estimation strategies: structural zeros 
in an MCMC MLE framework (the mtergm function can do this) and MPLE with 
bootstrapped confidence intervals (use the btergm function to do this). 
The latter is faster but becomes more accurate and less biased with 
larger networks and more groups); the former is more accurate with 
smaller numbers of groups but also prohibitively slow for more than a 
couple of networks. Of course, you can also construct a block-diagonal 
matrix with off-diagonal structural zeros manually and then use the ergm 
package, which is basically what mtergm does for you.

Note, however, that the ERGM or TERGM does not solve the problem with 
the violation of the i.i.d. assumption for you; you must explicitly 
control for network dependencies in your groups for an ERGM to yield 
results that are less biased than a GLM. In other words, just adding 
density and node attributes is likely not enough.

Best,
Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Fabian,

Is the advice of a pupil to a pupil equivalent to the advice of a
professional to a professional? (Is Xij = 1 qualitatively the same
relationship as Xim = 1? With "i" and "j" being pupils and "m" being a
professional?)

If this is not the case, what you describe sounds to me like a multilevel
network. Here you have both, the unipartite structure of ties between nodes
of the same type (your pupil to pupil advice) and the bipartite structure
of ties between different types of nodes (often used to express affiliation
to organizations - but could also express advice from qualitatively
different types of nodes). It is possible but not necessary to allow links
between the other type of nodes.
It sounds to me that the relationships here are qualitatively different
between different types of nodes but if you simply code them in one matrix
the program cannot see that and they would contribute to the statistics in
the same way that pupil-pupil ties do.
Example: You observe  the following constellations pupil1 -> pupil2, pupil1
-> pupil3, pupil2 -> pupil3 and professional1 -> pupil1, professional1 ->
pupil2. These 5 ties look like 2 transitive triads, however, the triad with
the professional involved should probably not count to the same triad
statistics as the triads with only pupils involved.

Unfortunately I do not have hands on experience with multilevel networks in
statnet. The ERGM package is able to model bipartite networks (I did not
find anything about multilevel) and I assume there is a way to model
multilevel networks in the statnet packages (otherwise MPNet might be an
alternative).

Eventually, I recommend using a multiplex multilevel network. Statnet is
able to handle multiplex networks (multiplex means different types of edges
between nodes).
This, I think, would capture the data in the way you describe it.

For further reading on multilevel networks I recommend this book:

Multilevel Network Analysis for the Social Sciences.

Emmanuel Lazega and Tom A.B. Snijders (eds).

Cham: Springer, 2016. Methodos Series: Methodological Prospects in the
Social Sciences.

ISBN 978-3-319-24518-8

ISBN 978-3-319-24520-1 (eBook)

DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-24520-1

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

messages.body_plain:
Hi Robert and Fabian,

This may or may not be necessary depending on the statistics to be used. 
Some statistics like triangle have an 'attr' argument where you can 
specify that only within-type triangles should be counted. However, I 
think this was not implemented for GWESP and related statistics. In 
principle, it should be possible to use a standard ERGM (with 
off-diagonal structural zeros) with some custom model terms where you 
restrict the counts of subgraph products to be established only within 
or across levels of an optional nodal attribute. If you don't want to 
code them in C (in case they don't have such an argument), you can still 
code them up as a change statistic manually and include them as a dyadic 
covariate.

Kind regards

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] unanswered statnet question
messages.body_plain:
Hi Katherina,

Sorry for not responding earlier.  We did in fact spend some time on 
this, and it led to two different streams of responses.  Since the two of 
us involved were also teaching a workshop last week, this response was 
delayed.

The two things we noticed were:

1. The issue with convergence has to do with changes in the way that 
ergm handles estimation with missing data.  We had already been working on 
that, and the tests with the pre-release version of ergm (planned for 
release before Sunbelt) and several different seeds suggests that 
convergence is obtained for your example.

2. The gwodegree term is not providing a good fit to your data, largely 
because your odegree distribution is bimodal.  try:

barplot(summary(n ~ odegree(0:20)))

to see this.  In general, when using the gw* terms, it is a good idea to 
look at the corresponding *degree or *sp distributions first, to see if 
they are distributions that have the form that gw* terms are designed to 
summarize -- a monotonic pattern of decline in the upper tail.  In your 
case, the odegree dist'n has a secondary mode in the upper tail.

The gw* terms may also induce degeneracy in an ergm when there is 
mis-specification like this.  So, even if your model converges, the lack 
of fit may mean it is converging to a degenerate model:  the realizations 
from the model are bimodal, with neither mode centered on the observed 
sufficient statistics, but the average of the two modes matches these 
statstics.

If the paragraph above doesn't make sense to you, i'd suggest taking a 
look at Mark Handcock's classic working paper on ergm degeneracy here:

https://www.csss.washington.edu/research/working-papers/39

Your question led me to develop some exploratory approaches to the 
gw*terms that i'll be posting on the statnet site soon.

HTH.

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Microstructure of brokerage
messages.body_plain:
Hello


I am looking at absorptive capacity in open innovation collaborations. Essentially absorptive capacity is a form of organisational learning where knowledge acquired by individuals is transformed into new ideas/innovations at the group and organisational level.  I believe brokerage is a key social mechanism in absorptive capacity and I would like to analyse this in terms of the conduit, tertius gaudens and terius iungens processes as outlined by Obstfeld, Borgatti and Davis (2014).


I have directed knowledge provider networks from three open innovation case studies with codifiability, observability and complexity of knowledge provided rated on a scale of 1 to 10 (three measures of tacitness).  Using exponential random graph models, I want to see how patterns of brokerage differ with different levels of tacit knowledge sharing in an open innovation collaboration. My goal is to look at absorptive capacity at the level of the collaboration as well as at the firm level.


I am presented with a challenge of specifying network triadic microstructures of interest (namely the tertius gaudens/iungens orientations).


I reckon I can use two-paths (021C) to describe conduit processes and two paths (021D) with a tail  to describe tertius gaudens processes, and triads (120D) with a tail to describe tertius iungens processes.  I would like to examine these in purely structural terms or consider these microstructures with each node having an attribute = membership of a particular organisation. However, I am not sure how easy it will be to interpret the over/under representation of these configurations.


The ergm.graphlets package looks interesting but does not seem to support directed networks? Any advice would be appreciated.


Kind regards

--
Andrew Terhorst
Open Innovation Researcher
Location leader for Sandy Bay site

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Microstructure of brokerage
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Andrew -

It is not obvious how one would be able to infer matchmaking brokerage 
from cross-sectional data, since it cannot be distinguished from any 
other form of clustering (and, in some cases, eliminates the evidence of 
its own pre-condition - i.e., after i brokers the formation of the {j,k} 
edge, the {i,j} and {i,k} edges may break).  I can imagine some very 
clever tricks using supplemental data in special cases, but as a general 
matter I suspect that it is impossible.  If you are interested in 
detecting the evidence of processes like matchmaking, you are going to 
need dynamic data.  (See e.g. Spiro et al. (Social Networks, 2013) for a 
discussion of some of the issues involved in assessing dynamic versus 
static brokerage.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter
